fatal_errors: The proposed heat-treatment intervention does not reconstruct the modulation-period comparison among coherent, semicoherent, and grain-boundary-dominated multilayers.

The hypothesized 900 °C creep regime is incompatible with the target room-temperature, 5 mN nanoindentation-creep regime and lacks evidence that the approximately 1 μm coating remains structurally stable there.
The governing target mediator—semicoherent FCC/BCC interfaces with misfit dislocations—is replaced by unestablished precipitates and serrated grain boundaries.
The experiment bundles precipitate formation and boundary serration, so it cannot determine which feature governs any observed improvement.
Failure of the heat treatment to produce the intended microstructure would be an intervention failure, not a valid falsification of the proposed mechanism.
explanation: The hypothesis is testable and broadly plausible for elevated-temperature HEA creep, but it is not a reconstruction of the target mechanism. The target varies multilayer period and finds optimum resistance at 16 nm semicoherent interfaces, with low stress exponents suggesting diffusion or interface slip after dislocation pileup and possible interfacial amorphization. The generated account instead introduces heat-treatment-induced L12 precipitates or serrated boundaries and predicts conventional high-temperature rupture behavior. Its untreated control is reasonable internally, but it does not include the coherent-interface and grain-boundary-dominated target baselines. E2 supports serrated-boundary benefits in a bulk additively manufactured HEA at 650 °C, while E1 concerns gamma/gamma-prime superalloy simulations; neither directly establishes these structures or effects in the stated FCC/BCC coating. A stronger test would independently vary precipitate density and boundary serration, verify each mediator before loading, and falsify the mechanism if successfully modified samples show no creep benefit after controlling for phase fraction, grain size, and hardness.
